title: Musharakah: A Teacher's Manual
subtitle: From the first definition to the governance rules. Master course, edition 7 (2026).
One of the core contracts of Islamic finance.

blocks.x: How to use this manual

**Who it is for.** A teacher who will explain musharakah to people who work in finance but know no Arabic and nothing of Islamic law. The manual assumes no prior knowledge. Every Arabic word is explained the first time it appears and is listed in the glossary (Part 8).
**How it is built.** Eight parts, each building on the last:

i: The word and the idea
Musharakah in academic terms: what kind of contract it is, and why it is allowed
The rules, with every school's position
Musharakah in practice: how it is used today
Governance: what the regulators and standard-setters say
Teaching aids: worked cases, review questions, common mistakes
The scholars and works quoted
Glossary

blocks.x: **How sources are shown.** Every rule carries its source in brackets: the author and the page, or the standard and the clause. For example "(Usmani, p. 24)" or "(AAOIFI SS 12, 3/1/5/4)". **Hadith** (reports of what the Prophet Muhammad said, did or approved) are cited by collection and report number. Quotations from al-Kafi, Tanwir al-Miqbas and Ma'arif al-Qur'an are from English translations. Where a report's grade is given, it is the grade in the edition used, unless a grader is named. Quotations from Arabic books with no English edition named are this manual's own translations. Where a quotation is this manual's own translation although an English edition exists, it is marked "this manual's translation". Where the scholars or schools disagree, every view is given with the name of the person or school who holds it. No view is presented as "the" answer. Where an author gives his own opinion, it is marked as his.

**Words used throughout.** *Shari'ah* is Islamic law as a whole; *fiqh* is that law as the jurists work it out. The *Sunnah* is the Prophet's example, known through hadith. The *Companions* are the people who knew the Prophet and followed him. A *caliph* is a leader of the Muslim community after the Prophet. *Sunni* and *Shia* are the two main branches of Islam. In the Shia branch, an *Imam* is one of the leaders from the Prophet's family whose reports carry authority. Among Sunnis, *Imam* is also a title of respect for a leading scholar, as in "Imam Malik" or "Imam Ahmad". A *dirham* was a silver coin and a *dinar* a gold coin; the classical books state cash amounts in them. *Fulus* were copper coins. Dates are given in the common era (CE) unless marked **AH**: years of the Islamic lunar calendar, counted from the Prophet's emigration to Medina in 622 CE.

**The schools named in this manual.** Islamic law has several schools (in Arabic *madhhab*, plural *madhahib*). Four are Sunni and are named after early jurists: the **Hanafi** (Abu Hanifah, d. 767), **Maliki** (Malik ibn Anas, d. 795), **Shafi'i** (al-Shafi'i, d. 820) and **Hanbali** (Ahmad ibn Hanbal, d. 855). The main Shia school is the **Ja'fari** or **Imami** school (from *Imam*, because it follows the Imams of the Prophet's family), named after Ja'far al-Sadiq (d. 765). Ibn Hazm (d. 1064), a defender of the **Zahiri** ("literalist") school, is named where he holds a view. The Qur'an commentator al-Tabari (d. 923) is known as an independent jurist (*mujtahid*), and is named for his reading of a verse. He is often said to have founded a school of his own, the **Jariri** (from his name, Ibn Jarir), though this is not certain.
**Suggested teaching plan.** Six sessions of about 90 minutes:

The evidence, the pillars, the kinds of partnership
Guarantees, management, ending, the special kinds
Bank finance, diminishing musharakah, criticism, musharakah sukuk

Part 1. The word and the idea
1.1 The problem musharakah solves

A person with money has two honest choices, in Usmani's account. If he wants to **help** someone, he can lend and take back only what he lent. If he wants to **earn** from someone's business, he can join it as a partner, and then he shares in its losses as well as its profits (Usmani, p. 18).

What he may not do is lend and ask for a fixed extra. That extra is **riba** ("increase"), which Islamic law forbids. Usmani argues that a fixed return is unfair both ways: if the business loses, the lender still takes his fixed amount; if it makes a large profit, the lender gets only a small fixed share of it (Usmani, p. 17). In the Islamic system, he writes, the person who puts money into a business bears the risk of loss and is entitled to "a proportionate share in the actual profit" (Usmani, p. 14).
Musharakah is the contract for that second choice: two or more people put money into one business and share what it actually earns.
1.2 The names

i: **Shirkah** (also read *sharikah*): "sharing" or "partnership". This is the word the classical books use for the whole subject. The Shafi'i commentary *Mukhtasar Tuhfat al-Muhtaj* says that in the language the word means mixing (*Mukhtasar Tuhfat* 2:251). Ibn Qudamah (Hanbali, d. 1223) gives the legal meaning: "coming together in a right to something, or in dealing with it" (*al-Mughni* 5:3).

**Musharakah.** Usmani notes that "the term 'musharakah' is not found in the books of Fiqh". Writers on Islamic finance brought it in, and they normally use it for one kind of shirkah: the partnership in capital, where two or more people invest in a joint business. Sometimes it also covers the partnership in services (Usmani, p. 20). This manual uses the word in that sense.
**Sharik** (plural *shuraka'*): a partner.
The Malaysian central bank spells the word **musyarakah**, and notes that "the terms of shirkah, sharikah and sharkah are synonymous to musyarakah" (BNM PD Musyarakah 2015, 10.1 and note 1).

1.5 A first picture

Amina puts in 60,000 and Bilal puts in 40,000 to open a shop. Bilal will run it. They agree to split the profit 50/50. - If the shop makes a profit of 20,000, each takes 10,000. - If the shop loses 10,000, Amina bears 6,000 and Bilal 4,000: loss follows the money each put in, whatever the profit split. - Is the 50/50 profit split valid, when Bilal put in only 40%? Part 2. Musharakah in academic terms
2.1 Two kinds of sharing: owning and contracting

The classical books divide shirkah into two kinds. Al-Kasani writes: "partnership in principle is of two kinds: partnership in things owned, and partnership by contract" (*Bada'i'* 6:56). Ibn Qudamah makes the same division (*al-Mughni* 5:3).

r: Two or more people own one thing together. It is ownership, not yet a business
By an act, such as buying, receiving a gift, a bequest or a charity together; or with no act, such as heirs who inherit together
People agree to run a business together for profit

blocks.x: The difference matters in law. Bank Negara Malaysia states that in shirkat al-milk "each partner's ownership is mutually exclusive", so one partner cannot deal with the other's share without consent, while in shirkat al-'aqd each partner is an agent for the others (BNM 11.1). AAOIFI's standard does not cover ownership partnership at all (AAOIFI SS 12, clause 1), and AAOIFI's new accounting standard leaves co-owned assets out of its scope too (FAS 51, para. 3(c)). The distinction comes back in diminishing musharakah (4.8), where a house bought jointly is a partnership in ownership.

2.3 Why it is allowed: the evidence
The sources agree that partnership is allowed in general. They differ on how strong each piece of evidence is, and on which kinds are allowed.
2.3.1 The Qur'an
Ibn Qudamah and Bank Negara Malaysia cite two verses, 4:12 and 38:24 (*al-Mughni* 5:3; BNM App. 1). AAOIFI cites only 38:24 (AAOIFI SS 12, App. B).

**Qur'an 4:12** is on inheritance: brothers and sisters through the mother who inherit together "share the third of the estate" (BNM App. 1, quoting the verse). Part 3. The rules, with every school's position

**Disputed: partnership with non-Muslims.** The worry in the classical books is that the non-Muslim partner may deal in riba or in goods Islam forbids, such as wine and pork.

Fungible goods (things measured, weighed or counted alike) cannot be partnership capital before mixing, "in the view of all of them", and goods of two different kinds cannot be either. For goods of one kind after mixing, Abu Yusuf says the partnership is not valid and they become only a partnership in ownership, while Muhammad says it is valid. So if two partners mix equal amounts of wheat and agree to split profit in thirds, Abu Yusuf divides the profit by the amounts and Muhammad by the agreement. blocks.x: **Copper coins (*fulus*).** Al-Kasani reports three Hanafi views. In the well-known narration from Abu Hanifah and Abu Yusuf, coins in circulation count as goods, so partnership in them is invalid. Muhammad (usually taken to be al-Shaybani, though this is not certain) holds it valid, because circulating copper coins function as money. A narration from Abu Yusuf allows partnership in them but not mudarabah (*Bada'i'* 6:59).

**The workaround.** Both Hanafi and Shafi'i texts describe the same way round the rule: each owner sells half (or part) of his goods for half of the other's, so that they own all the goods jointly, and then they make the partnership (*Bada'i'* 6:59; *Mukhtasar Tuhfat* 2:253). The Shafi'i text adds that the sale must not be made conditional on the partnership, and that partners who already own fungible property jointly, for example by inheritance or purchase, complete a partnership simply by giving each other permission to trade with it (*Mukhtasar Tuhfat* 2:253).
3.2.2 Debts as capital

**A debt is not capital** for al-Kasani, AAOIFI and Bank Negara Malaysia. Al-Kasani requires the capital to be "present property", not a debt and not property that is absent, because profit comes from dealing and one cannot deal with a debt; the Hanafis require it to be present at the time of buying, not at the time of the contract (*Bada'i'* 6:60). AAOIFI does not allow capital made up of receivables alone, but allows debts that are an inseparable part of the assets put in (AAOIFI SS 12, 3/1/2/4). Its reason: debts owed to a partner "cannot actually be used in partnership operations, as they are not assets in possession" (AAOIFI SS 12, App. B). Bank Negara Malaysia: "All forms of debts shall not qualify as capital, including all account receivables and payments due from other partners or third parties" (BNM 15.5).

**What a partner may do.** AAOIFI lists the ordinary acts of trade each partner may do, starting with "spot or deferred sales", but not gifts or loans unless all partners agree; small short-term loans of the usual kind are allowed (AAOIFI SS 12, 3/1/3/1). blocks.x: Part 4. Musharakah in practice
4.1 Why it is called an ideal tool

Usmani gives an example of what goes wrong with interest. Owners put in 10% of a project's money; the other 90% comes from a bank lending its depositors' money. If the project does very well, the depositors get only a small fixed interest, and almost all the profit goes to the owners. If it fails, most of the loss falls on the bank and its depositors. Musharakah would pass a fair share of the real profit to the depositors through the bank (Usmani, pp. 17-18).

Usmani also writes that other Islamic tools, such as *murabahah* (a sale at cost plus an agreed profit) and leasing, "are not ideal modes of financing" and should be used only where musharakah and mudarabah cannot work (Usmani, pp. 12-13). Islamic financing, he adds, is always tied to real assets: swapping money for more money of the same currency is riba, so profit must come from something with real use (Usmani, p. 12).
4.2 The four principles for bank financing

The classical books mostly picture a venture that starts, trades and is wound up. Modern businesses run on while partners come and go. Usmani's point is that the details may change as long as four principles stay (Usmani, pp. 37-38):

i: **Financing is not lending.** It is joining the business and owning part of its assets in line with the money put in.
**The financier shares in loss** up to the amount he financed.
**Profit ratios are agreed freely** and may differ from capital shares, but a partner excluded from all work may not take more than his capital share.
**Loss is always shared exactly by capital.**

blocks.x: Principle 3 matches the rule AAOIFI attributes to the Hanafi and Hanbali schools (3.3.2). The Maliki and Shafi'i texts quoted in 3.3.2 require profit to follow capital.
4.3 Financing a project, and how the bank gets out

i: Both sides put in money: **musharakah**.
The bank pays for the whole project: **mudarabah** (see the mudarabah manual).
Both put in money but only one manages: **musharakah and mudarabah combined**.

blocks.x: Because the partnership starts on day one, there is no problem valuing the capital, and profit can be counted by normal accounting (Usmani, p. 38).

**The exit.** The client may buy the bank's share at an agreed price. If he cannot pay all at once, the bank's share is divided into smaller **units**, sold one at a time, until the bank is out. The bank's share may also be sold to a new partner (Usmani, pp. 38-39). The IFSB asks banks to define their exit routes for equity investments in advance (IFSB-1, Principle 3.3).
4.4 Musharakah certificates

A large project can raise money from the public. Each subscriber gets a **musharakah certificate** showing his share in the project's assets. A bond is a loan that must be repaid, usually with interest; a certificate is a share of ownership (Usmani, p. 39).
Can the certificates be traded above face value? It depends on what the project holds (Usmani, pp. 39-41):

r: Only cash, or money owed to it
**Not allowed.** The certificate stands for money, and selling money for more money is riba. Only at face value
Mainly real assets (land, buildings, machines, stock)
**Allowed** at any agreed price, like any goods
A mix of cash and real assets

blocks.x: On the mixed case, as Usmani reports it:

i: **The traditional Shafi'i view:** not saleable unless the real assets are separated and sold on their own.

**The Hanafi view:** saleable, if the price is **more than** the cash part. Example: a Rs 100 certificate stands for Rs 60 of cash and Rs 40 of machines. It may be sold for any price above Rs 60; sold for Rs 110, Rs 60 pays for the cash and Rs 50 for the machines.

**"Most of the contemporary scholars", including Shafi'is:** trading is allowed only if real assets are "more than 50%" of the total. For trading "acceptable to all schools", real assets should be above that level; on the Hanafi view a smaller share is enough, but it "should not be negligible" (Usmani, p. 41).

blocks.x: 4.5 Financing a single deal: imports and exports

**Imports.** An importer asks a bank to finance one shipment. Banks usually support it with a **letter of credit** (a bank's promise to pay the foreign seller once the shipping papers are in order). The bank owns its share of the goods until they are sold, and the proceeds are split by the agreed ratio (Usmani, p. 42). If the goods are not sold by an agreed date, the importer may buy the bank's share, but at the market price on that day or a price agreed on that day, not a price fixed at the start (Usmani, p. 42).

**Exports.** The exporter has an order at a known price, so the expected profit is clear. The bank may require that the exporter alone bears a loss caused by his own mistakes in the shipping papers; other losses are shared, because the bank is a partner (Usmani, pp. 42-43).
4.6 Financing the working capital of a running business

**Method 1: value the business, then share the growth** (Usmani, pp. 43-45). The parties agree a value for the existing business; that value is the owner's capital (following Malik's view that capital need not be cash, 3.2.1). The bank's money is its capital. At the end of an agreed term the business is valued again and the gain is shared. Classically, profit is known only once everything is sold; Usmani's view is that an agreed valuation can count as a "constructive liquidation", since nothing in the law forbids it.
Usmani's worked example (pp. 43-44): the owner A's business is worth 30 units; the bank B adds 20 units, so A owns 60% and B 40%. They agree that B gets 20% of the profit.

r: The business grows to 100 units (a gain of 50)
The gain follows the profit ratio, 20/80: B gets 10
The business falls to 40 units (a loss of 10)
The loss follows the capital ratio, 40/60: B bears 4

blocks.x: B is a non-working partner who takes less profit than his capital share. The views in 3.3.2 that require profit to follow capital would not allow this split; the others would.

**Method 2: share gross profit only** (Usmani, pp. 46-47). Valuing a whole factory is hard and leads to disputes. The partners may instead share **gross profit**: income less only the **direct** costs of the deal (raw material, direct labour, power used). The owner carries the **indirect** costs (building, machinery wear, office staff) himself, because he uses them for his other business too. In return he may take a higher share of the profit, or an agreed rent for his building and machines.

**Method 3: a running account, profit by "daily products"** (Usmani, pp. 47-52). Banks often let a business draw and repay money at any time. Usmani proposes treating such an account as a musharakah: each partner's capital is counted by the money he had in the pool each day, and profit is worked out per unit of money per day. He adds that "this suggestion needs further consideration and research by the experts of Islamic jurisprudence" (Usmani, p. 48).

i: *First objection:* this is an estimate, not the real profit each person earned. *Usmani's answer:* once a pool exists, all its profit belongs to all partners, whosever money was used. His Hanafi example: A and B agree to put Rs 50,000 each into a 50/50 partnership; B buys and sells air-conditioners at a Rs 10,000 profit before A's money comes in; A's money then buys refrigerators sold at a Rs 2,000 loss. The total profit is Rs 8,000, and A still gets Rs 4,000 (Usmani, pp. 49-50).

*Second objection:* in a running account no one knows the capital in advance. *Usmani's answer:* the Hanafis do not require it (al-Shafi'i does), and al-Kasani says uncertainty spoils a contract only if it leads to disputes (Usmani, pp. 50-51; see 3.2.4).

blocks.x: AAOIFI's newer accounting standard treats this "running Musharaka" as the most common form of a "variable-equity" venture, which its older standards did not cover (FAS 51, definitions (g) and IN5(c)).
4.7 Common worries, and Usmani's answers
Usmani accepts that musharakah is harder to run than a loan, and answers each worry (Usmani, pp. 52-56):

r: **Risk of loss.** Depositors will avoid banks that may lose their money

Banks already study a business before lending; with musharakah they study it harder. A bank holds many partnerships, so losses in some are covered by profits in others. Profit is the reward for bearing some risk

Strong audit; sharing gross profit (4.6) to leave less room for disputes; penalties for proven cheats. Banks can start with clients of known honesty, and with exports, where prices and costs are clear
**Business secrets.** A bank partner may learn them
The client can require that the bank stays out of management and shares nothing without permission
**Clients will not share profit**, and some fear the tax office will learn their true profit

Clients should be persuaded that "borrowing on interest is a cardinal sin, unless there is a dire necessity", and that expanding a business is not such a necessity; banks and clients should press for fair tax rates

blocks.x: He adds that Islamic banks were set up to build a new system, not only to make money, and should start using true musharakah, at least "on a selective basis" with clients of known integrity (Usmani, p. 55).
4.8 Diminishing musharakah

In a **diminishing musharakah** the bank and the client own something together, and the client buys the bank's share bit by bit until he owns all of it (Usmani, pp. 57-64). The bank's share is divided into units, bought on a schedule.
4.8.1 Three examples (Usmani, pp. 57-59)

i: **House.** The client pays 20% of the price and the bank 80%. The client lives in the house and pays rent for the bank's share. The bank's share is cut into 8 units; every 3 months the client buys one, and the rent falls with each purchase. After 2 years he owns the house.
**Taxi.** A pays 20% and B 80%. The fares are split by ownership; as A buys B's units, A's share of the fares grows.
**Business.** A puts in 40% and the financier B 60% of a garments business. B's share is cut into 6 units, which A buys over two years while profit is shared.

blocks.x: 4.8.2 The pieces of a house deal

Usmani breaks a house deal into separate steps: a joint purchase; the bank leasing its share to the client; the client's promise to buy the units; each purchase on its own date; and a lower rent as the bank's share falls (Usmani, pp. 59-60).

**Joint purchase** is a partnership in ownership (2.1). **Leasing a share to the partner** is allowed by all the jurists, Usmani writes. Leasing an undivided share to an outsider (a third party) is disputed: he reports that Abu Hanifah and Zufar do not allow it, while Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Yusuf and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan (usually taken to be al-Shaybani, though this is not certain) do (Usmani, p. 60). The standards allow either partner to rent the other's share (AAOIFI SS 12, 5/9; IIFA Resolution 136; BNM 22.4).
4.8.3 The key rule: no contract may be a condition of another

Each step is allowed on its own, but it is "a well settled rule", Usmani writes, "that one transaction cannot be made a pre-condition for another", so the steps must not be tied together (Usmani, p. 60). The way round it is a **one-sided promise**: the client promises to rent the bank's share and to buy the units later. Is such a promise binding? Usmani reports that many hold a promise to be only a moral duty, while some Maliki and Hanafi jurists let a court enforce it in cases of need, especially in trade; the Hanafis applied this to a sale with a separate promise to sell back, called *bay' bil-wafa* (Usmani, pp. 60-62). AAOIFI settles the point for this product in its standard on promises: the bank's promise to lease its share to the client, and the client's promise to buy units of the bank's share at stipulated intervals, "are legally binding" (AAOIFI SS 49, section 5, the clause on diminishing musharakah). A legally binding promise is enforceable only against the one who made it; the other party may demand performance or waive it (SS 49, 3/5). Bank Negara Malaysia's policy document on promises gives a worked example for diminishing musharakah: the customer promises to buy the bank's share gradually during the financing and wholly on default, and the bank promises to sell its share to the customer on early settlement (BNM PD Wa'd 2017, Example 3; also para. 13.7).
All the standards keep the pieces apart:

i: AAOIFI: the buying and selling "should not be stipulated in the partnership contract"; the buying partner gives "only a promise to buy" (AAOIFI SS 12, 5/1).
The International Islamic Fiqh Academy: the contracts and commitments "should be kept independent from each other" (IIFA Resolution 136).
IFSB: the customer's binding promise is "in a separate document", and each buy-out is "in accordance with a separate contract of sale entered at that time" (IFSB-23, para. 205).

blocks.x: **For the teacher.** AAOIFI, the Fiqh Academy and the IFSB all ban a buy-out at the original, face or nominal value; Bank Negara Malaysia bars a buy-out of a venture that results in a guarantee of capital. They differ on **when** an agreed price may be fixed. AAOIFI and the Fiqh Academy speak of a price agreed at the time of each purchase. The IFSB speaks of a price agreed at the date of contracting. Bank Negara Malaysia allows "any price to be agreed" for an asset, and for asset financing requires the price to be fixed at the start on the purchase price; for a venture it speaks of a price agreed at the time of purchase (23.2, 23.4). Usmani allows a price fixed in the promise for a house; for a business he says the price cannot be fixed in the promise to purchase, allows two options, and finds only valuation at each purchase practical. This manual does not settle the point; a product must meet the rule of the framework that governs it.
4.8.5 Other rules on diminishing musharakah

i: AAOIFI does not allow a clause that one partner bears all the cost of insurance or maintenance because he will end up owning the asset (AAOIFI SS 12, 5/3); where either partner rents the other's share, each stays responsible for the periodic maintenance of his own share (5/9). The Fiqh Academy says such costs "should be charged to the Mushārakah account", by the partners' shares (IIFA Resolution 136).

The profit ratio may differ from the ownership ratio, and may be kept or changed as the shares change, but loss always follows the ownership shares (AAOIFI SS 12, 5/5); loss is borne periodically as the bank's share falls and the client's rises (5/4).
No clause may give a party the right to take back his capital (AAOIFI SS 12, 5/2; IIFA Resolution 136).

The rent falls with the bank's share (IFSB-23, para. 206(b)). In Malaysia, the formula for the bank's profit may use "a relevant pricing benchmark", such as the current rental rate, or "an Islamic reference rate", such as the Kuala Lumpur Islamic Reference Rate (BNM 32.5 and notes 52-53).
If the client breaks his promise to buy, Bank Negara Malaysia's rules depend on what the diminishing musharakah is for.

**For an asset** (such as a house), the partners may agree at the start that if a partner "breaches his promise to acquire the musyarakah asset as agreed or fails to pay his rental", the other "may sell the asset to that partner or to a third party" (BNM 22.9). In a sale to a third party after a breach of the promise, under Approach 1, the partners sell jointly; the proceeds are shared by ownership at the point of sale, either after deducting the costs of selling the asset or with those costs deducted from the client's share only; the bank may claim "the rental due (if any)" and "a compensation amount" from the client's share of the proceeds, the compensation being "the difference between the agreed purchase price (as promised) and the realised proceeds portion allocated for the promisee"; if the client's share is not enough, the bank may demand the remaining difference from him; if the bank's share of the proceeds reaches the promised price, there is no compensation, and any excess may be shared with the client. Under Approach 2, the bank sells its remaining share to the client "on credit based on a price agreed by both parties", and may take the asset as collateral; if it sells the collateral, it may claim "the rental due, the purchase price as agreed in the promise to purchase and c osts related to liquidation of the collateral" (as printed), may demand any shortfall, and any excess "shall belong to the promisor" (22.10). For an asset still under construction, the bank may compel the client to buy "based on the price agreed in the promise", and rent that the client paid under a forward lease (*ijarah mawsufah fi zimmah*) may be set off against the purchase price (22.12); once construction is complete, 22.9 applies (22.11).

**For a venture** (a business), the bank may "invoke the promise and compel the promisor to purchase the share at market value or fair value", or "sell the share to a third party and claim any actual cost incurred in the process from the promisor" (BNM 23.5).

**On default in musharakah financing**, the customer "shall have the first right of refusal to purchase the asset"; any sale to a third party must follow Shari'ah; the bank "shall not redeem such shortfall from the customer until the loss is realised"; and where the diminishing musharakah is arranged with ijarah, the bank may claim accrued rent only "if the customer is still enjoying the usufruct" (BNM 32.9).

4.10 Musharakah sukuk

**What they are.** *Sukuk* (singular *sakk*) are certificates of equal value, each representing "undivided shares in ownership of tangible assets, usufruct and services or (in the ownership of) the assets of particular projects or special investment activity"; AAOIFI adds that this is true "after receipt of the value of the Sukuk, the closing of subscription and the employment of funds received for the purpose for which the Sukuk were issued" (AAOIFI SS 17, clause 2). In musharakah sukuk the venture is a partnership. AAOIFI describes them as certificates issued to use the money raised for a new project, an existing project or a business activity "on the basis of any of partnership contracts", so that the holders "become the owners of the project or the assets of the activity as per their respective shares". The venture may be run as a partnership, as a mudarabah or by an investment agent (AAOIFI SS 17, 3/6). The issuer invites the subscribers into a partnership with him; the subscribers are the partners, the money they pay is their share of the capital, and they own the partnership assets "with the accompanying profits and losses" (SS 17, 5/1/5/6). The IFSB describes them as "the direct proportionate ownership shares of the holders in the assets of a private commercial enterprise or project" (IFSB-23, para. 650). The holders' money may buy fixed assets such as real estate, while the originator (the company raising the money) "can contribute specific assets or management skills" (para. 604). The Securities Commission Malaysia defines them as certificates "evidencing the certificate holder’s undivided ownership in the musharakah venture" (SC Guidelines on Islamic Capital Market Products and Services, para. 3.01).

Compare the musharakah certificates in 4.4. AAOIFI states that it is "permissible to trade in Mudarabah, Musharakah and investment agency certificates after closing of subscription, allotment of the certificates and commencement of activity with respect to the assets and usufructs" (SS 17, 5/2/16). On trading or redemption before the activity begins, the full sentence reads: "As for trading or redemption prior to the commencement af activity, it is necessary to observe the rules of the contract of Sarf (currency exchange) along with the rules for debts (receivables) when liquidation is complete and the assets are receivables er when the assets represented by the Suk:uk are sold for a deferred price" (5/2/1, as printed). The sentence can be read in two ways: the two "when" cases may belong to the rule before the activity begins, or they may be cases in which the debt rules apply whenever they arise. This manual does not choose between the readings. This manual adds a comparison of its own, which SS 17 does not make (SS 17 does not mention face value): in Usmani's table in 4.4, certificates that stand only for cash or money owed trade at face value.

**The basic partnership rules still apply, but not always in the same words.** AAOIFI: the prospectus must state that each holder shares in profit and bears loss in proportion to the value of his certificates (SS 17, 5/1/8/6). That clause opens "Taking into account item 3/1/5 of the Shari'ah Standard No. (12)", and in SS 12 profit "may be in proportion" to each partner's capital, but "the partners may agree to make profit-sharing not proportionate to their contributions to capital, provided the additional percentage of profit over the percentage of contribution to the capital is not in favour of a sleeping partner" (SS 12, 3/1/5/3). The Securities Commission's rules for sukuk musharakah: capital in cash, in kind, or both (26.51); at least two partners to form the musharakah, but "no minimum number of musharakah partners (i.e. investors) in the secondary market" (26.52); profit by the pre-agreed ratio, while "any loss must be shared among the partners according to their respective capital contribution" (26.53); and the venture may be managed by "one of the partners or issuers or a third party" (26.54). So the texts on profit read differently: SS 17 ties the holders' profit to the value of their certificates, while referring to the SS 12 item that allows an agreed ratio; the Securities Commission allows a pre-agreed ratio, which may later be revised (26.63). This manual does not settle how SS 17, 5/1/8/6 and SS 12, 3/1/5/3 fit together for sukuk. The Shariah Advisory Council also recognises two forms (SC SAC Resolutions, 2023, pp. 124-126). In the first, the issuer and the investors are partners, and the issuer is also the manager. In the second, the partnership is among the investors only (at least two); "Normally sukuk issuer will only act as a manager on behalf of the investors"; and "If the issuance of sukuk musharakah is made in tranches and under separate musharakah contracts, then each musharakah contract shall has at least two investors or more at all times" (p. 125, as printed).
**The key question: can the holders' capital be protected?** Here the frameworks differ.

r: The prospectus may not say that the issuer will compensate the holder "up to the nominal value" except for wrongful acts and negligence, nor that he guarantees a fixed percentage of profit. An independent third party may give a guarantee "free of charge", and the issuer may give security against its own wrongful acts or negligence

For tradable sukuk, the issuer may promise to buy any certificate offered to him "at market value", but "it is not permissible for the issuer to undertake to purchase the Sukuk at their nominal value"

It is not permissible for the *mudarib*, *sharik* (partner) or *wakil* (agent) "to agree to purchase assets from Sukuk holders or from whoever represents them for a nominal value of those assets" when the sukuk end. The manager does guarantee the capital at its nominal value "in cases of negligence or mala fides or non-compliance with stated conditions"

A partner may not "undertake in advance to repurchase the assets at maturity ... for their nominal or par value"; a purchase "on the basis of the net value of assets, their market value, or fair value, or a price to be agreed at the time of purchase" is allowed. **Risk management (IFSB-1, 2005).** Banks need strategies, risk management and reporting for equity investments, "including Mudarabah and Musharakah investments" (Principle 3.1); valuation methods that are appropriate and consistent (Principle 3.2); and exit strategies defined in advance (Principle 3.3). The IFSB notes that in musharakah the bank "may be silent partners, or may participate in management" (para. 48).
**Capital adequacy (IFSB-23, December 2021).**

i: **Equity risk weights.** A bank applies a **250% risk weight** to musharakah or mudarabah investments in commercial enterprises, or **400%** to short-term unlisted equity exposures (IFSB-23, para. 204). In plain words: the bank bears loss like a shareholder, so it holds much more capital against a musharakah than against an ordinary loan.
**Capital is at risk.** IFSB-23 treats the capital invested in a musharakah as exposed to impairment (paras. 201-202).

**Diminishing musharakah.** The bank has two exposures. (a) The amounts the partner owes to buy out the units on their dates are a credit risk; the credit exposure is the remaining balance of the amount invested, at historical cost, less specific provisions (para. 206(a)). (b) The bank's share of the income from the asset, such as lease rentals, is also a credit risk, for non-payment of the rentals; the rent "is adjusted periodically to reflect the IIFS's remaining ownership share" (para. 206(b)). If a third party gives an undertaking, its risk weight may be used, and the undertaking should be free of charge (note 97). The default clause may let the bank end the partnership and require the partner to buy the whole remaining share, though a partner in distress may be unable to (note 96).
**Diminishing musharakah on a leased asset.** Treated like a musharakah with a leasing subcontract: the lessee's risk weight, plus 100% on the residual value (para. 207).

**Shari'ah rules repeated.** A partner cannot guarantee another's capital, and the buy-out price may not be the nominal value (para. 393(c)(ii)-(iii), in section 4.3.2.4; 4.8.4).

**Musharakah sukuk.** No advance promise by a partner to buy back at nominal or par value; purchase at net asset value, market value, fair value or a price agreed at the time of purchase is allowed (para. 603); a musharakah sukuk may use a repurchase undertaking on those terms (para. 604). Holdings are treated as equity-like positions, with risk weights by what the venture does (paras. 650-654; see 4.10).

Separately, AAOIFI reports that the United Arab Emirates adopts its Shari'ah standards "as mandatory regulatory requirements" (AAOIFI, "Adoption of AAOIFI Standards" web page). **On that report, a UAE musharakah product would be tested against AAOIFI SS 12 (5.1), within the CBUAE governance structure and the HSA's rulings.**
5.5 Saudi Central Bank (SAMA)

SAMA's Shariah Governance Framework for Local Banks Operating in Saudi Arabia was issued in February 2020. It covers the duties of the board and executive management, the Shariah committee (formation, membership, duties, independence), internal control, Islamic window operations and the process for developing Shariah-compliant products. It contains no rules specific to musharakah and does not name a contract standard for it. **A Saudi musharakah product is therefore reviewed by the bank's own Shariah committee under this framework.**
5.6 Securities Commission Malaysia

**Who it is.** Bank Negara Malaysia's policy document (5.3) applies to Islamic financial institutions such as Islamic banks (BNM 4.1, 7.2). It covers products structured on musyarakah "except for : (i) sukuk, collective investment schemes and equities; and (ii) interbank investments , which are excluded from Part C and D" (BNM 4.1(b)). A sukuk issuer must lodge (file) the sukuk with the Securities Commission, after first obtaining its Shariah Advisory Council's endorsement (SC Guidelines, 26.01). The Commission's Shariah Advisory Council (SAC) was set up on 16 May 1996 and, under the Securities Commission Malaysia Act 1993, is the authority on how Shari'ah principles apply to Islamic capital market business (SC website, "Members of the Shariah Advisory Council").

**The text used here.** The Guidelines on Islamic Capital Market Products and Services (SC-GL/1-2022), first issued on 28 November 2022 and revised on 8 February 2024 and 30 March 2026. Chapter 26 sets the Shari'ah requirements for ringgit-denominated sukuk, including musharakah sukuk.
**Key requirements (Chapter 26).**

i: **Endorsement.** An issuer must get the endorsement of the SAC before lodging a sukuk with the Commission (26.01), and again for any change to the principal terms and conditions (the main terms of the issue) that has a Shari'ah implication (26.02).

**Shariah adviser.** The adviser must issue a Shariah pronouncement giving its reasoning for the structure, confirming that the proceeds are for Shari'ah-compliant purposes, and naming the rulings and concepts used (26.05).
**Proceeds and venture.** The proceeds must be used for Shari'ah-compliant purposes only (26.06); in sukuk musharakah, "the ventures or investment must comply with Shariah" (26.08).

**Partnership rules for sukuk musharakah.** Capital in cash, in kind or both (26.51); at least two partners (26.52); profit by the agreed ratio and loss by capital (26.53); a partner, the issuer or a third party as manager (26.54).
**Guarantees.** Who may guarantee what, and the fee rule (26.18-26.20, 26.22); set out against AAOIFI and the IFSB in 4.10.

**Purchase undertakings.** The Shariah Advisory Council allows them, as a binding promise outside the sukuk contract, with the exercise price set by an agreed formula or at the sale (SAC Resolutions, 2023, pp. 129-130; see 4.10).
**Compensation, waiver, revisions and naming** (26.16, 26.25, 26.61, 26.63, 26.65, 26.32): see 4.10.

6.1 Case studies
*All five cases are illustrations made for this manual.*

**Case 1: The guaranteed partner.** A bank puts 600,000 into a trading business as a musharakah partner, alongside the owner's 400,000. The term sheet says: "The owner guarantees the return of the bank's capital in all cases."
*Questions:* Is the clause valid? What can the bank ask for instead?

*Discussion points:* No partner may guarantee another's capital (AAOIFI SS 12, 3/1/4/1; BNM 15.14, 18.1, 27.36; IFSB-23, para. 393(c)(ii)). The bank may take security for misconduct, negligence or breach (AAOIFI SS 12, 3/1/4/2; BNM 18.2(a)), or an independent third-party guarantee (AAOIFI SS 12, 3/1/4/3, which also requires it to be free of charge; BNM 18.3, which requires a separate contract, use to cover loss or depletion of capital, and a guarantor who is not a related party). Compare the two sets of independence tests, and BNM's list of excluded guarantors in Part C (27.42).
**Case 2: The silent partner's share.** Amina puts in 60% and Bilal 40% of a venture. The contract says Amina will never work and takes 70% of the profit.
*Questions:* Which sources allow the 70% share? Would the answer change if the contract were silent about Amina's work?

*Discussion points:* Not valid where profit must follow capital (Malik in the *Mudawwana*; the Shafi'i texts; Zufar; Ibn Hazm). For the Hanafis, al-Kasani holds a larger share for the non-working partner invalid (*Bada'i'* 6:63), and Usmani gives Abu Hanifah's sleeping-partner limit (p. 24); Ibn Qudamah, by contrast, reports Abu Hanifah as allowing any agreed ratio (*al-Mughni* 5:23). AAOIFI bans the extra for a sleeping partner but allows it for a partner who has not stipulated that he will not work (SS 12, 3/1/5/3). The Hanbalis allow any agreed ratio (*al-Mughni* 5:23). BNM: proportional unless agreed otherwise at the start (16.2). See 3.3.2.
**Case 3: The machinery as capital.** A factory owner wants to put his machines into a musharakah as his capital; the bank puts in cash.
*Questions:* Which schools allow it? How should the machines be valued? Is there a workaround for those who refuse?

*Discussion points:* 3.2.1 in full. Malik (*Mudawwana* 3:605); Ahmad's two narrations (*al-Mughni* 5:13); al-Kasani for "the general body of scholars" (*Bada'i'* 6:59); the Shafi'i rule on fungible goods (*Mukhtasar Tuhfat* 2:252). AAOIFI (3/1/2/1) and BNM (15.2-15.3) on valuation. The workaround of selling halves to each other (*Bada'i'* 6:59; *Mukhtasar Tuhfat* 2:253). Usmani's working-capital method 1, which values the existing business as the owner's capital (pp. 43-45).

**Case 4: The home finance buy-out.** A bank and a client buy a house 80/20 under diminishing musharakah. The draft promise says the client will buy each unit "at one-eighth of the bank's original contribution".
*Questions:* Is that price allowed under AAOIFI, the Fiqh Academy, the IFSB and BNM? What does Usmani say?

*Discussion points:* AAOIFI, the Fiqh Academy and the IFSB ban a buy-out at original, face or nominal value (AAOIFI SS 12, 5/7; IIFA Resolution 136; IFSB-23, para. 393(c)(iii)). BNM bars a gradual buy-out of a venture that results in a guarantee of capital, and sets its price at market value, fair value or a price agreed at the time of purchase (23.2-23.3). For an asset it allows "any price to be agreed by the partners" (22.5), and in asset financing it requires the price to be fixed at the start, based on the purchase price, with a formula for each redemption (32.3-32.4). If the client breaks the promise, BNM's remedies also differ for an asset (22.9-22.12) and for a venture (23.5) (4.8.5). The frameworks also differ on when an agreed price may be fixed (4.8.4). Usmani allows a price fixed in the promise for a house (p. 62); for a business he says the price "cannot be fixed in the promise to purchase", allows two options, and finds only valuation at each purchase practical (pp. 63-64). AAOIFI makes the client's promise to buy units legally binding (SS 49, section 5). Ask learners whether "one-eighth of the original contribution" is a face-value price.
**Case 5: The overdraft as partnership.** A bank lets a trader draw and repay at will, and proposes to share profit by "daily products".
*Questions:* What are the two objections, and how does Usmani answer them? Which accounting standard covers it?

*Discussion points:* Usmani, pp. 47-52 (4.6). The capital-knowledge debate (3.2.4): Hanafis and the Shafi'i "sounder view" versus al-Shafi'i as reported by al-Kasani. FAS 51 on running musharakah (definitions (g), para. 59).
6.2 Review questions (with answers)

i: **What is the difference between shirkat al-milk and shirkat al-'aqd?** The first is owning something together; the second is a business partnership made by contract (*Bada'i'* 6:56; BNM 11.1).
**Is the word "musharakah" found in the classical law books?** No; Usmani says writers on Islamic finance brought it in (p. 20). The books use *shirkah*.
**How is loss shared?** By capital, for every holder in 3.4. Usmani: "loss is always subject to the ratio of investment" (p. 25).

**Which schools allow a profit ratio different from the capital ratio?** The Hanbalis; Abu Hanifah, as reported by Ibn Qudamah (any agreed ratio); the Hanafis as stated by al-Kasani, and Abu Hanifah as summarised by Usmani (with the limit on a non-working partner); AAOIFI and BNM. Not Malik, al-Shafi'i, Zufar or Ibn Hazm.
**Is "A gets 15% of his investment" valid?** No: profit must be a percentage of actual profit, not of capital (Usmani, p. 23; AAOIFI SS 12, 3/1/5/1).
**May a partner guarantee another partner's capital?** No (AAOIFI SS 12, 3/1/4/1; BNM 18.1; IFSB-23, para. 393(c)(ii)).
**Which four kinds of contract partnership do the classical books discuss, besides mudarabah?** *'Inan*, *mufawadah*, *abdan* (work) and *wujuh*.
**Which kind does the Shafi'i school accept?** Only *'inan* (*Mukhtasar Tuhfat* 2:252).
**What does al-Qurtubi say about reading *khulata'* in Qur'an 38:24 as "partners"?** That it is "far-fetched"; most scholars, he reports, take it to mean owners whose herds are kept together.
**Can a managing partner be paid a salary?** Not under the partnership contract itself (AAOIFI SS 12, 3/1/3/4), but yes under a separate contract (AAOIFI SS 12, 3/1/3/5; BNM 14.4).
**What risk weight does IFSB-23 give a musharakah investment in a commercial enterprise?** 250%; 400% for a short-term unlisted equity exposure (para. 204).
**When does FAS 51 replace FAS 4?** For financial statements beginning on or after 1 January 2027 (FAS 51, paras. 74, 76).

**May the issuer of a musharakah sukuk promise to buy the certificates back at their nominal value?** Not under AAOIFI (SS 17, 5/2/2; the 2008 statement) or the IFSB (IFSB-23, para. 603). The Securities Commission's Shariah Advisory Council allows purchase undertakings, with the exercise price set by an agreed formula or at the sale, and does not speak of nominal value; the Commission's guidelines set out who may guarantee the capital (SC Guidelines, 26.22) (4.10).
